name: Special Pleading
statement: Special pleading is applying a rule to everyone except oneself or one's group, without a logically relevant reason for the exemption.
statementAccent: applying a rule to everyone except oneself or one's group
meaning: Special pleading is an informal fallacy in which someone insists a general rule applies to others but claims, without adequate justification, that their own case is an exception. It is fundamentally a double standard dressed up as a principled distinction. The fallacy lies not in claiming an exception exists, but in failing to give a reason for it that would count as relevant if anyone else made the same claim.
mechanism: The arguer relies on a general principle, then, when it counts against their own position, invokes a supposedly special circumstance to exempt themselves, but the circumstance is not one they would accept from an opponent. This asymmetry, relaxing a standard for oneself while holding others to it, is what makes the reasoning fallacious rather than a legitimate distinction.

examples.text: A police association argued officers should not ticket other officers or their families for traffic violations. Being related to an officer is irrelevant to whether a law was broken, making this a textbook double standard.

Bertrand Russell argued that insisting "everything has a cause" but exempting God alone commits special pleading unless a relevant difference is shown; defenders reply the real claim is "everything that begins to exist has a cause," a distinct non-fallacious version.

Dismissing criticism by asserting "you can’t understand unless you’ve experienced what I have" grants oneself an exemption from answering the objection, without showing the experiential gap is actually relevant.

whyItMatters: Special pleading lets people evade accountability by quietly exempting themselves from standards they demand of everyone else, corroding fairness in law, ethics, and debate. Recognising it forces arguers to state what specifically makes an exception principled rather than self-serving.
limits: Not every claimed exception is fallacious: a case can genuinely differ in a way that matters, such as an on-duty officer’s emergency. The fallacy occurs specifically when no logically relevant justification is given, or the cited difference does not bear on the rule’s purpose.
misreadings: People confuse legitimate case-by-case reasoning (citing a relevant distinguishing factor) with special pleading (citing an irrelevant one); the test is whether the same exception would be accepted if made by an opponent.
origin: "Special pleading" began as a technical legal term for a pleading that introduced new justifying facts, drafted by specialists called special pleaders; it later migrated into general use for any argument that unfairly carves out a self-serving exception.
